Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I should have protected others and I failed

vignette: Luther, a 61‑year‑old bus driver who has spent more than three decades hauling passengers along the downtown corridor, first encountered the violence that would come to haunt him during a protest in his early twenties. While marching with a coalition of civil‑rights activists, he was seized by a paramilitary squad and taken to a clandestine facility where he endured hours of interrogation and physical torment. The memory of the stony walls, the metallic taste of blood on his lips, and the crackling of the electric shocks still flash in his mind in flashes of hyper‑clarity, yet many other moments remain shrouded, as if the darkness of the cell had erased them. He has never told a friend about the night he was left on a concrete slab, his throat raw, his body trembling; the experience became a fragmentary, terror‑laden recollection that feels both too vivid and disturbingly incomplete. Because the terror on recall is so intense, Luther finds his nights suffused with vigilance. He wakes repeatedly, heart hammering, and listens for the faintest creak of a door or the distant rumble of a truck, convinced a new threat is lurking just beyond his bedroom window. Whenever the sudden jolt of an alarm clock or the hiss of the kitchen stove triggers a flashback, his body reacts with a surge of adrenaline, his muscles tightening, his breath shallow. In these moments, the memory of his own helplessness in that cell resurfaces, making the present feel as if the walls of the interrogation room had collapsed around him. The terror he experiences at night is not a passive echo; it feeds back into the way he perceives the present, making every ordinary sound feel like a potential harbinger of the violence that once defined his life. The guilt that gnaws at Luther’s mind compounds his sense of danger. He believes he should have fought harder, that his inaction was a sign of weakness, and that he failed to protect not only himself but also the comrades he shared the protest with. These negative appraisals magnify the threat he feels in the dark; when he thinks of how he could have intervened, his anxiety spikes, and the very thought of walking into the night triggers a cascade of worry. At the same time, each nocturnal episode of alarm and panic reinforces his belief that he is inherently weak, that he cannot command his body to stay calm. In this way, the fear he experiences at night does not simply mirror his memory; it becomes a self‑reinforcing echo that deepens his negative self‑evaluations. Luther’s perception of the incomplete picture of his trauma further entangles him in a cycle of self‑blame. The parts of the event that remain blank compel him to fill the gaps with the narrative of a failed protector, thereby strengthening his inaction guilt. As he reconstructs those missing moments, the sense that he was powerless or that he could not have done more takes root, shaping how he remembers the whole ordeal. The gaps, the missing details, and the terror that still grips him when he tries to recall the incident all feed back into the same loop of guilt and perceived weakness. For years, Luther has carried this loop into his daily life as a bus driver. When his route crosses the quiet, dimly lit avenues of the city at night, he finds himself unable to focus on the road, his hands trembling as he steers. The fear of a sudden threat at the wheel forces him to shorten his evening shift, which in turn causes tension at home with his wife, who worries that he is avoiding the night altogether. It is this mounting strain—on his job, his relationships, and his own sense of safety—that finally drives Luther to seek help. He hopes that by confronting the memories he keeps shivering from, he can quiet the night‑time vigilance and regain the confidence he once believed he lacked, and he fears that without intervention, the cycle will only tighten, robbing him of more moments with his family and his livelihood.
